target.title: Shared equipment turnaround
target.frame: A municipal maintenance depot lends specialist equipment to four crews. During the last six weeks, 19 of 74 bookings started late although the booking calendar showed the equipment available. Return times, cleaning completion and collection times are recorded in separate logs; some entries are missing. The depot manager has two weeks to choose changes that reduce late starts without buying equipment or adding staff. Work out what to investigate and how to decide which change to trial.

instrument.state: The underlying process may change over time, and a single observation cannot adequately distinguish stable state, transient fluctuation, or directional change.
instrument.operation: Repeat a comparable measurement or observation at multiple time points and evaluate the resulting sequence against expected variation or a defined change rule.
instrument.signal: The sequence exhibits persistence, trend, reversal, threshold crossing, or another temporal pattern not available from an isolated measurement.
instrument.inference: The temporal pattern constrains hypotheses about whether and how the underlying state is changing and can distinguish sustained change from some forms of transient variation.
instrument.limit: Measurement error, regression to the mean, irregular sampling, changing measurement conditions, interventions between observations, and poorly chosen intervals or thresholds can create or conceal apparent trends.

P001.text: Act on the equipment turnaround process across the four crews, treating each booking as one observation in a time sequence.

P002.text: The reported 19 late starts among 74 bookings establish an aggregate problem, not whether it is persistent, worsening or temporary.

P003.text: Possible contributors include late returns, cleaning delays, inaccurate availability entries and delayed collection; these are hypotheses.

P004.text: Missing entries and separate logs may obscure the sequence.

P005.text: During the two-week investigation, link the preceding six weeks of bookings to return, cleaning-completion and collection records by equipment and booking, retaining missing values explicitly.

P006.text: Agree consistent definitions of scheduled start, ready for collection and actual start; do not equate collection with actual start unless that relationship is verified.

P007.text: For every new turnaround, record these events comparably, plus expected return where available, calendar changes and exceptional circumstances.

P008.text: Identify whether equipment was absent, awaiting cleaning or ready but uncollected at the scheduled start; leave ambiguous cases unresolved.

P009.text: Review daily and summarize each week using late bookings divided by all bookings, delay minutes, stage-specific counts and recording completeness.

P010.text: Compare comparable equipment and crew groups before pooling them.

P011.text: Before inspecting the prospective sequence, adopt this provisional persistence rule: a candidate bottleneck must recur on multiple booking days in each investigation week, with the same stage accounting for the greatest documented delay burden in both weeks.

P012.text: At day 14, choose a feasible change aimed at that stage: for example, revise return handoffs, reserve observed turnaround time in the calendar, or introduce a readiness-and-collection handoff.

P013.text: These options remain conditional on findings and must fit existing equipment and staffing.

P014.text: If missing records could reverse the ranking, or bookings are too sparse to apply the rule, choose a standardized recording and handoff trial first rather than claim a bottleneck is established.

P015.text: Look for repeated stage-specific delays, consecutive elevated weekly late-start rates, increasing delay duration, reversals, or isolated spikes followed by recovery.

P016.text: Show booking denominators and missing-record counts alongside each time point.

P017.text: A meaningful candidate signal would be a recurring readiness delay despite calendar availability, or repeated late collection after documented readiness.

P018.text: These are observations to seek, not findings already obtained.

P019.text: Historical weeks provide context only where definitions and coverage are comparable.

P020.text: Repeated comparable observations can support distinguishing an enduring turnaround constraint from a short-lived disruption and can narrow which operational change deserves a trial.

P021.text: Persistent delay at one stage supports targeting that stage; a rise confined to one equipment type or crew supports a narrower trial.

P022.text: After selection, continue the same measurements through a predefined trial period, preferably staggering introduction across comparable bookings where practical.

P023.text: Sustained improvement across repeated periods would support retaining the change, while isolated improvement would warrant continued observation.

P024.text: Timestamp errors, missingness, irregular booking frequency, changing job mix, workload, measurement practices and concurrent interventions can create or hide patterns.

P025.text: Two weeks and small subgroup counts may be insufficient; the persistence rule is a practical selection rule, not statistical proof or causal identification.

P026.text: Test whether plausible assignments of unresolved cases alter the decision.

P027.text: Set trial success and acceptable service-impact thresholds before implementation.

P028.text: Stop or revise a trial if it causes unsafe handoffs or unacceptable disruption; extend observation when evidence is sparse.

P029.text: Check that apparent improvement does not merely shift starts later, suppress bookings or move delays to other crews.

instrument.state: A reproducible failure occurs for a configuration or input composed of multiple removable parts, and candidate reductions can be repeatedly tested.
instrument.operation: Partition the failure-inducing configuration, remove subsets or test their complements, and iteratively retain reductions that continue to reproduce the defined failure.
instrument.signal: Some reduced configurations preserve the failure while others do not, revealing which removals are compatible with continued reproduction.
instrument.inference: The procedure narrows the configuration to a test-relative minimal or near-minimal failure-inducing subset or difference whose retained parts are sufficient to reproduce the observed failure under the test.
instrument.limit: Interactions among parts, nondeterministic failures, unresolved test outcomes, environmental dependence, and the reduction strategy can prevent strong minimization. A retained minimal configuration demonstrates reproducibility under the test, not necessarily the unique underlying causal mechanism.

P001.text: Treat a reconstructed equipment turnaround as the candidate failure-inducing configuration: preceding bookings, return timing, cleaning requirements, readiness updates and collection handoffs.

P002.text: These are candidate components, not established causes.

P003.text: During days 1–3, link the 74 bookings to the separate logs by equipment and booking, retaining missing or conflicting entries as unknown.

P004.text: Define failure as a booking starting after its agreed start time despite the calendar showing availability; distinguish equipment unreadiness from delayed crew collection.

P005.text: Establish how actual starts were measured.

P006.text: Select a late case for which a tabletop or controlled operational replay can repeatedly reproduce that failure.

P007.text: Replay feasibility and fidelity must be demonstrated, not assumed.

P008.text: During days 4–9, partition the selected case's candidate components into groups.

P009.text: Test removing a group or retaining its complement, keeping the equipment, agreed start deadline and other test conditions fixed.

P010.text: Give each removal an explicit operational counterpart: for example, remove an earlier booking from a replay, eliminate a redundant handoff, or replace delayed readiness communication with an immediate update.

P011.text: Removing an earlier booking is diagnostic and does not by itself justify reducing service.

P012.text: Never remove required cleaning or safety checks, and do not erase missing records to manufacture a passing test.

P013.text: Retain a reduced configuration only when repeated tests still reproduce the defined failure; then partition it again.

P014.text: If neither groups nor complements yield a reproducing reduction, test smaller removals.

P015.text: Use the same predeclared repetition rule for baseline and reduced configurations, and classify uncertain timing, missing prerequisites or inconsistent outcomes as unresolved.

P016.text: Stop when no single remaining component can be removed while preserving failure, when further reductions are unsafe or infeasible, or at the end of day 9.

P017.text: For each tested configuration, record retained and removed components, return and cleaning completion, readiness communication, collection and start times, deviations from the intended test, and whether failure reproduced, did not reproduce, or remained unresolved.

P018.text: The informative pattern would be a smaller configuration that repeatedly remains late while specified further removals cease to reproduce lateness.

P019.text: Compare reconstructed on-time bookings to check whether the replay has omitted relevant operating conditions.

P020.text: A replay that cannot reproduce the baseline supplies no basis for reduction; investigate its missing conditions instead.

P021.text: A consistently reproducing reduction would identify a test-relative sufficient combination for the selected failure.

P022.text: Only exhaustive single-component removal checks justify calling it locally minimal; otherwise report it as near-minimal or merely reduced.

P023.text: During days 10–14, translate the smallest supported combinations into feasible changes, such as an explicit readiness handoff or a turnaround allowance, only where the tests support those counterparts.

P024.text: Test the proposed change against the unreduced baseline scenario as well: eliminating failure in a reduced case alone is insufficient.

P025.text: Choose a bounded trial that addresses a supported combination, covers several reconstructed late cases, and fits existing equipment and staff.

P026.text: If evidence remains unresolved, choose a limited logging and readiness-verification trial to establish testability rather than assert a remedy.

P027.text: Historical reconstruction and tabletop replay depend on assumptions; agreement with recorded cases does not establish field effectiveness.

P028.text: Interactions, variable return times, missing entries, replay artifacts and partition order can produce different minimal subsets.

P029.text: A retained subset is neither necessarily unique nor proof of an underlying causal mechanism, and one case need not explain all 19 late starts.

P030.text: Before the field trial, fix its duration, comparison bookings and success rule using existing-service deadlines; track late-start frequency and minutes alongside completed bookings, workload, safety and displaced demand.

P031.text: Stop or reverse the trial if required safety work is compromised or agreed service or workload limits are exceeded.

P032.text: Do not count relabelled availability or shifted deadlines alone as improvement.

P033.text: Review at the trial's end; inconsistent results require more observation or a revised test, not rollout.

instrument.state: A claim or event description is supported by one or more information sources whose accuracy, independence, or access may be uncertain.
instrument.operation: Compare the claim against other independently sourced information while assessing each source's credibility, access, dependence, and relevance.
instrument.signal: Independent sources converge on, contradict, or fail to support the same material features of the claim.
instrument.inference: Genuine convergence across credible independent sources increases support for the corroborated features, while contradiction or lack of independent support lowers confidence or identifies unresolved uncertainty.
instrument.limit: Sources may share an undisclosed common origin, copy one another, inherit the same bias or error, have unequal access, or converge because of common assumptions rather than independent observation. Multiple reports therefore do not automatically constitute independent evidence.

P001.text: Act on the reported 19 late starts among 74 bookings over six weeks and on competing explanations for why calendar availability did not translate into timely starts.

P002.text: Treat delayed returns, unfinished cleaning, inaccurate availability updates and delayed collection as hypotheses, not established causes.

P003.text: Assume records can be linked to equipment and bookings; verify this first.

P004.text: Distinguish scheduled start, physical return, cleaning completion, readiness for collection, collection and actual work start.

P005.text: Establish what the reported 'late start' measures and use the existing lateness rule, or agree one before comparison if none exists.

P006.text: During days 1–4, assemble booking-level timelines from the calendar and separate return, cleaning and collection logs.

P007.text: Review all 19 reported late cases and use the remaining bookings to check whether suspected problems also occur without lateness.

P008.text: Preserve missing entries and uncertain matches explicitly.

P009.text: For each material claim, record who observed what, when it was recorded, whether the source had direct access, and whether it copied another record.

P010.text: Seek independently grounded checks through existing crew and depot accounts or contemporaneous records where available; ask about specific events before presenting a proposed explanation.

P011.text: During days 5–8, prospectively check disputed handoff points within existing staffing, using separate firsthand observations where feasible.

P012.text: Reconcile conflicting timestamps, definitions and equipment identities without forcing agreement.

P013.text: By days 9–10, compare candidate changes against the corroborated failure patterns, their frequency and delay burden, operational feasibility and possible effects on other crews.

P014.text: Conditional candidates include a turnaround allowance for verified return-to-ready delays, a readiness confirmation before calendar release for verified status errors, or a collection handoff rule for verified collection failures.

P015.text: Select one narrowly scoped, reversible trial by the two-week deadline; do not combine changes whose effects could not be distinguished.

P016.text: Look for independent agreement or disagreement about the same equipment, booking and handoff.

P017.text: For example, a return entry and a separately recorded firsthand observation could support that equipment arrived after the next scheduled start; a cleaning entry and an independent readiness check could support that cleaning remained incomplete at that time.

P018.text: Calendar availability alone does not establish physical readiness.

P019.text: Record contradictions, unsupported intervals and missing coverage alongside supported sequences.

P020.text: Count supported patterns across bookings and note whether similar patterns occur among timely bookings.

P021.text: For the selected trial, prospectively observe late-start frequency and delay duration, readiness and collection times, completed or displaced bookings, and any added workload or unmet cleaning requirements.

P022.text: Convergence among credible sources with independent access increases support for the specific corroborated timing or status feature.

P023.text: Repeated supported sequences can justify prioritizing a corresponding change for trial, especially when their timing plausibly explains the delay and comparison bookings strengthen that explanation.

P024.text: Favor the feasible change addressing the largest credible, avoidable delay burden without purchasing equipment or adding staff.

P025.text: Contradictions lower confidence and direct follow-up toward the disputed handoff.

P026.text: If no explanation has adequate independent support by the deadline, select a limited readiness-confirmation trial primarily to resolve uncertainty, explicitly leaving its delay-reduction benefit unestablished.

P027.text: Compare trial outcomes with comparable baseline bookings, accounting for equipment, crew and demand differences; improvement supports continued testing but does not alone establish causation.

P028.text: Separate logs are not necessarily independent: they may share an author, copied timestamps, clock errors or assumptions.

P029.text: Retrospective accounts may share a narrative, and missingness may be concentrated in busy or delayed periods.

P030.text: Absence of an entry does not prove that an event failed to occur.

P031.text: Corroborated timing does not by itself establish the cause of lateness, and readiness, collection and work start are different events.

P032.text: Stop treating a disputed feature as established when source dependence, poor access or unresolved contradictions undermine it; retain competing explanations.

P033.text: Before trial launch, specify its duration, comparable bookings, success criterion and acceptable workload and access effects.

P034.text: Stop or revise the trial if it compromises required cleaning, safe use or essential crew access, or requires extra staffing.

P035.text: If too few comparable bookings occur, extend observation within existing resources rather than claim success or failure from inadequate evidence.

instrument.state: Several plausible explanations can account for an uncertain situation, and available evidence may fit more than one of them.
instrument.operation: State the competing explanations explicitly, evaluate each item of evidence against all of them, emphasize evidence that is inconsistent with particular explanations, and test the sensitivity of the resulting comparison to uncertain evidence or assumptions.
instrument.signal: The evidence forms a comparative pattern of consistency and inconsistency across the competing explanations, with some items discriminating among them more strongly than others.
instrument.inference: Explanations with greater important inconsistency can be weakened or eliminated, leaving a smaller set of alternatives that better survives the observed evidence.

P001.text: Act on existing export records and traces, distinguishing the stable median from the reported roughly one-in-twenty exports exceeding an hour.

P002.text: Compare explicit, potentially coexisting explanations: queue congestion or worker shortages; worker-version regressions; slow or retried object reads; slow archive uploads; and workspace size or composition differences.

P003.text: Treat these as hypotheses, not findings.

P004.text: Trace coverage varies by worker version; availability of comparable timestamps, workload metadata and resource metrics remains uncertain.

P005.text: First examine existing slow and ordinary overnight exports without requesting customer reruns.

P006.text: Where available, compare exports with similar workspace size, object count, execution window and worker version; retain unmatched cases with their limitations.

P007.text: Separate queue wait, worker execution, object-read and upload durations only where trace semantics permit.

P008.text: Build an evidence-by-hypothesis matrix, marking each item consistent, inconsistent or unknown for every explanation and recording reliability and diagnostic value.

P009.text: Prioritize contradictions over counts of supporting items: for example, reliably short queue waits would weaken queue congestion as the direct source of an hour-long export.

P010.text: Avoid treating nested spans or multiple symptoms of one event as independent evidence.

P011.text: Repeat the comparison excluding incomplete traces, varying uncertain phase boundaries, stratifying by version and workload, and considering combined causes.

P012.text: If existing evidence cannot discriminate, propose a small canary deployment adding missing phase timing and coverage metadata, with bounded sampling and logging overhead and no document contents.

P013.text: Use normal overnight traffic; introduce controlled test exports only if representative test data and spare capacity are established.

P014.text: Before deployment, define acceptable instrumentation overhead, error rate, completion rate and tail-delay bounds against comparable baseline traffic.

P015.text: Halt expansion and revert the canary if those bounds are breached or monitoring cannot enforce them.

P016.text: Expand a targeted mitigation only when reliable discriminating evidence favors its mechanism and the canary meets those bounds; otherwise retain the current deployment and gather the specific missing evidence.

P017.text: Look for comparative patterns rather than a single suspicious trace.

P018.text: Long queue waits with ordinary post-start durations would favor queue-related delay and weaken downstream-only explanations.

P019.text: Ordinary queue waits followed by prolonged read or upload phases would discriminate in the opposite direction, provided those phases are measured comparably.

P020.text: A version association that persists within comparable workloads and execution windows would support a version-related hypothesis; an association that disappears after accounting for coverage or workload would weaken it.

P021.text: These are proposed observations, not results.

P022.text: Record whether the ranking changes when uncertain evidence is removed and whether the canary changes the predicted phase and overall tail without increasing failures or unfinished exports.

P023.text: Weaken explanations that conflict with reliable, diagnostically important observations; eliminate one only within the scope where its necessary prediction was adequately tested.

P024.text: Use the surviving alternatives to choose the next deployment: a bounded mitigation or rollback canary when evidence supports a specific mechanism, an instrumentation canary when observability is the main obstacle, or no behavioral change when uncertainty or operating risk remains too high.

P025.text: A successful mitigation canary would support expanding that action within tested conditions, while leaving open alternative explanations for the improvement.

P026.text: If reliable observations contradict every listed explanation, expand the hypothesis set before choosing a behavioral change.

P027.text: Missing spans are unknown evidence, not proof that a phase was fast.

P028.text: Incomplete exports may be absent from completed-export samples and must be accounted for where records permit.

P029.text: Version, workload and overnight load may be confounded; overlapping spans, inconsistent clocks, retries and dependent measurements can distort comparisons.

P030.text: Rare delays require enough comparable exposure to make absence informative, so a short clean canary cannot establish resolution.

target.title: Supplier approval records
target.frame: A nonprofit requires documented approval before staff place supplier orders above an internal spending threshold. A quarterly review found that 14 of 90 sampled orders lack an approval attachment in the purchasing system. Approvals may also be recorded in meeting minutes or delegated-authority forms. The operations lead must prepare a defensible account of what happened and decide which records or process changes to pursue before the board review in three weeks. The internal rule is given; no legal conclusion is requested.

instrument.state: An internal structure cannot be sampled directly, but variations within it systematically alter the propagation of signals that cross it along many paths.
instrument.operation: Measure signal travel behavior across many source-to-receiver paths, compare those observations with predictions from a candidate internal model, and iteratively adjust the model to reduce the discrepancies.
instrument.signal: The observed propagation times or waveforms differ from model predictions in spatially structured ways across the sampled paths.
instrument.inference: The pattern of discrepancies constrains a spatial model of internal properties that could have produced the observed propagation behavior.
instrument.limit: Sparse or uneven path coverage, measurement error, uncertain source locations, regularization choices, model assumptions, and non-uniqueness can create artifacts or allow multiple internal structures to fit the observations.

P001.text: Act on the sampled orders and the documentary traces linking approval decisions, order placement and purchasing-system records.

P002.text: The historical approval process is not directly observable; reconstruct it through multiple record paths.

P003.text: The packet establishes that 14 of 90 sampled orders lack purchasing-system approval attachments, but does not establish that approval was absent.

P004.text: Verify which orders exceeded the threshold and what the internal rule required at the time.

P005.text: Assume only provisionally that records can be linked and their dates interpreted reliably.

P006.text: During week one, build a candidate model of how documented approval should precede an order and reach the purchasing record, including any permitted routes through meeting minutes or delegated-authority forms.

P007.text: For each of the 14 flagged orders, trace paths from the purported approval through relevant records to order placement and attachment.

P008.text: Use the other sampled orders to test whether these routes also explain apparently complete records.

P009.text: Record order identifiers, amounts, approval content, applicable authority, event dates, record-creation dates and attachment dates, distinguishing these dates explicitly.

P010.text: A delegation form may establish authority without documenting approval of a particular order.

P011.text: During week two, compare observed links, timing and missing traces with each route's predictions.

P012.text: Investigate discrepancies through targeted record requests and staff clarification; treat recollections as leads rather than equivalent to contemporaneous documentation.

P013.text: Iteratively revise the candidate account and check its predictions against additional traces.

P014.text: Track alternative explanations rather than adjusting the account merely to make every order appear compliant.

P015.text: Observe whether predicted approval records can be found, linked to the relevant order and shown to precede placement, and whether their recorded authority fits the applicable rule.

P016.text: The counterpart to propagation behavior is the timing and continuity of documentary traces across approval-to-order-to-system paths.

P017.text: Look for structured discrepancies by approval route, responsible role, period or record location: for example, linked prior approvals without attachments, attachments without demonstrated prior approval, or repeated breaks at a particular handoff.

P018.text: These are proposed observations to test, not findings.

P019.text: Record searches that yield no result together with their scope and access limitations.

P020.text: Use the pattern of discrepancies to constrain competing accounts of where the process departed from its predicted route: obtaining approval, documenting it, linking it to an order, or attaching it to the system.

P021.text: Reliable evidence of appropriately authorized, documented approval before placement can support satisfaction of the given approval rule even when an attachment is missing, subject to the rule's actual record requirements.

P022.text: An attachment alone does not establish timely approval.

P023.text: An unsuccessful search supports 'approval not located within the searched sources,' not automatically 'approval never occurred.' Seek further records that distinguish competing accounts.

P024.text: Before the board review in week three, prepare an order-level evidence table separating supported conclusions, unresolved cases and alternative explanations; propose record corrections or process changes tied to the supported failure points.

P026.text: Standardizing all orders into one assumed workflow could conceal legitimate routes or manufacture apparent failures; retain exceptions and test assumptions.

P027.text: Multiple historical processes may produce the same surviving records.

P028.text: Do not infer a population failure rate from 14 of 90 without a defensible sampling basis, and do not make legal conclusions.

P029.text: Stop an individual inquiry when sufficient reliable evidence resolves the applicable rule or when identified sources are exhausted and the remaining uncertainty is documented.

target.title: Customer onboarding drop-off
target.frame: A business scheduling product has many new accounts but fewer first published schedules than expected. Interviews from eight customers mention confusing setup, missing team information and postponement until the next roster cycle. Event logs record account creation, invitations, draft saves and publication, but do not capture offline preparation. The product team has one small release slot this month and needs a plan for deciding what to change and how to learn whether it helps.

instrument.state: A sample contains multiple components whose interactions with two phases differ enough that those components need not move together.
instrument.operation: Carry the sample through a system containing a moving phase and a stationary phase so that components repeatedly partition between them.
instrument.signal: Components migrate at different rates and emerge at different positions or times, producing separated bands or detector peaks.
instrument.inference: The separation pattern supports the presence of distinguishable components with different partition behavior and permits their relative retention to be characterized.
instrument.limit: Components with similar partition behavior may co-elute, operating conditions can shift retention, detector response may be nonspecific, and retention behavior alone generally does not establish chemical identity without appropriate standards or orthogonal evidence.

P001.text: Act on a prospective cohort of newly created accounts, treating onboarding trajectories as a mixture of potentially distinguishable behaviors.

P002.text: Confusing setup, missing team information and waiting for a roster cycle are hypotheses suggested by eight interviews, not established segments or prevalence estimates.

P003.text: Assume accounts may repeatedly alternate between active product work and preparation or waiting; test that assumption rather than assigning each account a fixed cause.

P004.text: Use the same onboarding pathway and observation conditions across the initial cohort.

P005.text: Define the moving-phase counterpart as active work through invitations, draft saves and publication; define the stationary-phase counterpart as relatively persistent setup requirements and readiness constraints that can retain accounts before further progress.

P006.text: At successive milestones and a consistently timed inactivity follow-up, combine existing events with brief questions about the next required action, information availability, offline preparation and intended roster date.

P007.text: Record repeated progress–waiting–return transitions, allowing multiple or unknown reasons.

P008.text: Follow accounts through their stated next roster opportunity plus a predeclared grace period; use a fixed maximum follow-up for unknown dates and mark unfinished trajectories as censored.

P009.text: Before reviewing results, set minimum evidence and practically worthwhile improvement thresholds.

P010.text: Use the single small release slot for the smallest change addressing a recurrent, independently corroborated, product-addressable retention point: clearer instructions for verified comprehension problems, information collection support for verified preparation problems, or a timed return aid for verified postponement.

P011.text: If evidence does not distinguish an actionable constraint, use the slot for missing measurement instead.

P012.text: Where feasible, randomly assign eligible accounts to the selected change or the existing experience, keeping measurement identical.

P013.text: Stop recruitment and analysis at predeclared sample and follow-up limits; stop exposure early only under predefined harm criteria.

P014.text: Look for separated concentrations of trajectories in milestone position, time spent waiting, number of returns to active work and time to first publication.

P015.text: For example, renewed progress after obtaining team information or publication near a previously stated roster date would be candidate signals, not assumed observations.

P016.text: Report accounts with no return and incomplete follow-up alongside published accounts.

P017.text: In the release comparison, observe first-publication rates within a common window, time to publication, retention at the targeted checkpoint and predefined guardrails such as publication errors.

P018.text: Reproducible differences under common conditions would support distinguishable onboarding behaviors and characterize their relative retention at requirements or readiness constraints.

P019.text: Agreement between event patterns and contemporaneous preparation reports would strengthen a proposed mechanism.

P020.text: A sufficiently precise randomized improvement in first publication would support a causal effect of the tested change for the studied accounts and window; reduced delay at the targeted checkpoint would additionally support, but not establish, the proposed mechanism.

P021.text: Roll out only if the predeclared benefit and guardrail criteria are met.

P022.text: Otherwise retain the existing experience and use the uncertainty or conflicting evidence to specify the next targeted observation or test.

P023.text: Different causes can produce the same inactivity or publication timing, analogous to co-elution; one account can also experience several causes.

P024.text: Milestone events are nonspecific detectors, and absent events cannot distinguish abandonment from offline preparation.

P025.text: Added questions may change behavior, and self-reports may be incomplete.

P026.text: Roster timing, team size, acquisition mix and changes in onboarding conditions can shift apparent retention, so record these conditions and compare like observation windows.

P027.text: Behavioral retention alone does not identify a cause: seek corroboration through preparation reports, task observation or a controlled intervention.

P028.text: A small sample, sparse publications or censored accounts may leave effects unresolved; failure to meet the evidence threshold is not proof of no benefit.

P029.text: Without randomization, describe release differences as associations subject to confounding.

instrument.state: A sample contains multiple components whose interactions with two phases differ enough that those components need not move together.
instrument.operation: Carry the sample through a system containing a moving phase and a stationary phase so that components repeatedly partition between them.
instrument.signal: Components migrate at different rates and emerge at different positions or times, producing separated bands or detector peaks.
instrument.inference: The separation pattern supports the presence of distinguishable components with different partition behavior and permits their relative retention to be characterized.

P001.text: Act on a prospective cohort of newly created accounts, treating onboarding trajectories as a mixture of potentially distinguishable behaviors.

P002.text: Confusing setup, missing team information and waiting for a roster cycle are hypotheses suggested by eight interviews, not established segments or prevalence estimates.

P003.text: Assume accounts may repeatedly alternate between active product work and preparation or waiting; test that assumption rather than assigning each account a fixed cause.

P004.text: Use the same onboarding pathway and observation conditions across the initial cohort.

P005.text: Define the moving-phase counterpart as active work through invitations, draft saves and publication; define the stationary-phase counterpart as relatively persistent setup requirements and readiness constraints that can retain accounts before further progress.

P006.text: At successive milestones and a consistently timed inactivity follow-up, combine existing events with brief questions about the next required action, information availability, offline preparation and intended roster date.

P007.text: Record repeated progress–waiting–return transitions, allowing multiple or unknown reasons.

P008.text: Follow accounts through their stated next roster opportunity plus a predeclared grace period; use a fixed maximum follow-up for unknown dates and mark unfinished trajectories as censored.

P009.text: Before reviewing results, set minimum evidence and practically worthwhile improvement thresholds.

P010.text: Use the single small release slot for the smallest change addressing a recurrent, independently corroborated, product-addressable retention point: clearer instructions for verified comprehension problems, information collection support for verified preparation problems, or a timed return aid for verified postponement.

P011.text: If evidence does not distinguish an actionable constraint, use the slot for missing measurement instead.

P012.text: Where feasible, randomly assign eligible accounts to the selected change or the existing experience, keeping measurement identical.

P013.text: Stop recruitment and analysis at predeclared sample and follow-up limits; stop exposure early only under predefined harm criteria.

P014.text: Look for separated concentrations of trajectories in milestone position, time spent waiting, number of returns to active work and time to first publication.

P015.text: For example, renewed progress after obtaining team information or publication near a previously stated roster date would be candidate signals, not assumed observations.

P016.text: Report accounts with no return and incomplete follow-up alongside published accounts.

P017.text: In the release comparison, observe first-publication rates within a common window, time to publication, retention at the targeted checkpoint and predefined guardrails such as publication errors.

P018.text: Reproducible differences under common conditions would support distinguishable onboarding behaviors and characterize their relative retention at requirements or readiness constraints.

P019.text: Agreement between event patterns and contemporaneous preparation reports would strengthen a proposed mechanism.

P020.text: A sufficiently precise randomized improvement in first publication would support a causal effect of the tested change for the studied accounts and window; reduced delay at the targeted checkpoint would additionally support, but not establish, the proposed mechanism.

P021.text: Roll out only if the predeclared benefit and guardrail criteria are met.

P022.text: Otherwise retain the existing experience and use the uncertainty or conflicting evidence to specify the next targeted observation or test.

P023.text: Different causes can produce the same inactivity or publication timing, analogous to co-elution; one account can also experience several causes.

P024.text: Milestone events are nonspecific detectors, and absent events cannot distinguish abandonment from offline preparation.

P025.text: Added questions may change behavior, and self-reports may be incomplete.

P026.text: Roster timing, team size, acquisition mix and changes in onboarding conditions can shift apparent retention, so record these conditions and compare like observation windows.

P027.text: Behavioral retention alone does not identify a cause: seek corroboration through preparation reports, task observation or a controlled intervention.

P028.text: A small sample, sparse publications or censored accounts may leave effects unresolved; failure to meet the evidence threshold is not proof of no benefit.

P029.text: Without randomization, describe release differences as associations subject to confounding.

instrument.state: An item or record passes through multiple handlers or locations, creating opportunities for substitution, alteration, contamination, or uncertainty about identity.
instrument.operation: Record each transfer and handling event with the responsible party, time, and purpose, then inspect that history for continuity and unexplained transitions.
instrument.signal: A continuous, internally consistent handling record links the examined item through its lifecycle, while gaps or contradictions identify breaks in documented custody.
instrument.inference: Documentary continuity supports the claim that the item examined is the item collected and that its handling history is accounted for; gaps weaken that provenance claim.
instrument.limit: Complete documentation does not itself prove that handlers recorded events truthfully or that no unrecorded alteration occurred, and missing records do not prove that alteration occurred. The strength of the inference depends on the reliability of the recording and safeguarding process.

P001.text: Treat each new account’s path to its first published schedule as a history requiring traceable continuity across people, preparation steps and schedule versions. Account creation, invitations, draft saves and publication are documented event types; offline preparation is unobserved. Whether responsibility actually passes between people, which team information is required and when the account intends to publish remain questions to establish, not supplied facts.

P002.text: For a bounded cohort of new accounts, link existing events using account and schedule identifiers, checking that drafts and publications refer to the same schedule lineage.

P003.text: Record each relevant handling or handoff event with the responsible role, time, purpose, information or version passed, and intended next step.

P004.text: Use brief customer follow-ups to document offline preparation and intended roster timing, labeling retrospective reports and unknowns explicitly.

P005.text: Inspect histories for continuity, conflicting identities or versions, and unexplained transitions; ask the relevant participant to clarify gaps without replacing the original record.

P006.text: Use the eight interviews to suggest checks, not to establish prevalence.

P007.text: Spend the small release slot on one narrow change only if corroborated histories identify a recurring, actionable handoff problem—for example, an explicit missing-information checklist if that problem is confirmed.

P008.text: If histories remain unreliable or reveal no recurring actionable problem, stop short of selecting a presumed friction fix and use the slot to improve the deficient recording step.

P009.text: Before release, define eligible accounts, a common observation window covering their intended roster opportunity, first-publication outcome and recording checks.

P010.text: If feasible, randomly assign eligible accounts to the change or current flow; otherwise use a comparable contemporaneous cohort and document assignment differences.

P011.text: Follow unresolved histories through the agreed window and report accounts whose publication opportunity has not yet occurred separately.

P012.text: Look for an internally consistent sequence connecting account creation, responsible participants, preparation, invitations, draft versions and publication, with reported offline activity distinguished from logged events.

P013.text: Record missing links and contradictions as breaks in documented continuity.

P014.text: A documented wait until a stated roster date is an explained interval; silence alone is not evidence of postponement.

P015.text: After release, observe both whether the targeted handoff becomes more consistently accounted for and whether the proportion reaching a traceable first publication within the predefined window changes.

P016.text: These are proposed observations, not completed findings.

P017.text: A continuous history supports the claim that the examined publication belongs to the tracked account and schedule lineage and that its documented handling is accounted for.

P018.text: Corroborated histories may locate a recurring handoff suitable for the limited release; a gap initially warrants clarification or better recording, not attribution of a customer failure.

P019.text: Improved continuity supports better traceability, while increased first publication is a separate outcome.

P020.text: With valid random assignment, comparable follow-up and reliable outcome capture, a publication difference can support an effect of the change; without those conditions, treat the difference as an association and use clarified histories to guide further testing.

P021.text: Complete histories do not prove truthful reporting, correct identity linkage or absence of unrecorded offline work.

P022.text: Missing events do not prove abandonment, missing preparation or mishandling.

P023.text: The eight interviews cannot establish how common any explanation is.

P024.text: Intended roster dates may change, and accounts still awaiting their publication opportunity cannot yet establish failure to publish.

P025.text: Recording changes can create apparent improvement without changing customer behavior; verify linkage and capture comparability before interpreting results.

P026.text: Small cohorts, incomplete follow-up, differences between comparison groups and concurrent changes can leave the release effect uncertain.

P027.text: If these checks fail or evidence is too sparse, stop causal interpretation, retain the uncertainty and continue targeted follow-up or observation before deciding on another product change.

instrument.state: A set of observations can plausibly be explained by more than one underlying mechanism or condition.
instrument.operation: Generate multiple candidate explanations, gather or inspect evidence that bears differently on them, and repeatedly revise their relative plausibility as evidence accumulates.
instrument.signal: New observations create a pattern of support, contradiction, or non-discrimination across the competing explanations.
instrument.inference: Explanations can be reprioritized, eliminated, or retained, narrowing the plausible set without requiring an early commitment to a single cause.
instrument.limit: The result is constrained by which hypotheses were generated, the quality and independence of the evidence, test sensitivity and specificity, and susceptibility to anchoring, premature closure, base-rate neglect, or confirmation bias.

P001.text: Act on the path from account creation to a first published schedule.

P002.text: Retain competing explanations: setup confusion, unavailable team information, deliberate waiting for the next roster cycle, and alternatives such as exploratory accounts or unobserved technical failures.

P003.text: Mechanisms may coexist.

P004.text: The eight interviews suggest candidates but do not establish their prevalence; existing events omit offline preparation.

P005.text: Assume only provisionally that first publication represents useful activation, and check whether interviewed accounts actually intended to publish.

P006.text: First inspect account-level sequences of invitations, draft saves and publication, comparing accounts of similar age and checking event completeness.

P007.text: Recontact consenting customers sampled across different event paths, including publishers and non-publishers; ask when they intended to publish, what information was available, what preparation occurred offline, and where they stopped.

P008.text: Where feasible, observe a realistic setup attempt using information they already have.

P009.text: Seek evidence against each explanation as well as for it, and update an explicit explanation-by-evidence table after each batch.

P010.text: Use the release slot for one narrowly scoped change only if evidence identifies an actionable obstacle: for example, clearer guidance for observed comprehension failures, or a preparation checklist for uncertainty about required team information.

P011.text: If evidence instead supports intentional waiting, test an optional reminder near the intended roster date rather than assuming setup needs simplification.

P012.text: If evidence does not distinguish explanations, use the slot for a minimal diagnostic prompt or event improvement and defer a behavior-changing fix.

P013.text: For a selected change, randomly assign eligible new accounts to change or current experience if feasible.

P014.text: Before launch, specify eligibility, assignment, the primary first-publication measure, follow-up spanning an intended roster opportunity, a minimum worthwhile improvement, precision requirements and guardrails for errors, abandonment and unusable publications.

P015.text: Look for discriminating patterns rather than treating every unfinished funnel as the same failure.

P016.text: Difficulty proceeding despite ready team information, especially when clarified instructions resolve the difficulty, would support confusion.

P017.text: Understanding the steps but lacking necessary information, followed by progress when that information arrives, would support preparation dependency.

P018.text: A stated future roster date followed by publication around that date without setup assistance would support deliberate delay.

P019.text: Reproducible errors would support a technical explanation.

P020.text: These are proposed observations, not established findings.

P021.text: Draft saves, absent invitations or silence alone may fit several explanations.

P022.text: In the release test, observe the difference in first-publication rates over the specified follow-up, uncertainty around that difference, guardrails and intermediate behavior; collect brief explanations from a sample of continuing non-publishers.

P023.text: Reprioritize explanations as corroborating and contradictory evidence accumulates, retaining mixed causes where appropriate.

P024.text: Deprioritize an explanation only when the observation could reasonably have detected its predicted effect.

P025.text: A randomized improvement in useful first publication would support deploying that change for comparable accounts, while mechanism-specific observations would strengthen—but not prove—the proposed explanation.

P026.text: Intermediate progress without publication warrants further investigation, not a success claim.

P027.text: At the predefined endpoint, adopt the change only if the estimated benefit meets the decision criteria with adequate precision and acceptable guardrails; stop early for predefined material harm.

P028.text: If a precise result rules out worthwhile benefit, retire that intervention and revisit alternatives.

P029.text: If the result remains inconclusive, retain uncertainty and extend observation only under a predefined feasible extension; otherwise close the test as unresolved and choose the next discriminating inquiry.

P030.text: Conclusions depend on the candidate explanations considered, interview selection and recall, event accuracy, missing offline activity, and whether follow-up includes a genuine opportunity to publish.

P031.text: Eight interviews cannot estimate population prevalence.

P032.text: Multiple events from one account and several accounts from one organization are not independent confirmation.

P033.text: Diagnostic questions or observed assistance can change behavior.

P034.text: A small test, weak intervention, delivery failure or insensitive outcome can produce no detectable effect even when its mechanism matters.

P035.text: Without random assignment, differences may reflect account mix or roster timing rather than the release.

P036.text: Avoid anchoring by recording disconfirming evidence, checking representative frequencies before treating vivid cases as common, and reopening the hypothesis set when patterns remain unexplained.

P037.text: Do not generalize beyond the observed customer types and follow-up period.
